t.1.212.2: Permitted by Vāsudeva, having explained what was to be done, and having understood the mind of Kṛṣṇa, the bull of the Bharatas set out.
t.1.212.1: Then, when that had been agreed upon, Dhanaṃjaya, having received permission and having learned that the maiden had gone to Raivataka, O Janamejaya, set forth.
t.1.212.3: With a chariot whose parts were of gold, equipped according to rule, yoked with Sainya and Sugrīva, and garlanded with networks of tinkling bells.
t.1.212.4: With a chariot furnished with every weapon, resounding with the roar of thunderclouds, shining like a blazing fire, and destroying the joy of his enemies.
t.1.212.5: Armed and armored, bearing a sword, with leather finger-guards of iguana skin bound on, he set out at the same time under the pretext of hunting, O Bhārata.
t.1.212.6: Then Subhadrā, having worshipped Raivata, the lord of mountains, together with all the deities, and having had the brahmins pronounce blessings of well-being,
t.1.212.8: Then that tiger among men, taking her of the bright smile, set out for his own city in a chariot that seemed to travel through the sky.
t.1.212.7: Having circled the mountain, keeping it to her right, she set out toward Dvārakā; rushing upon her, the son of Kuntī forcibly lifted her onto his chariot.
t.1.212.9: But seeing Subhadrā being carried off, all the soldiery, crying out loudly, ran toward the city of Dvārakā.
t.1.212.11: Having heard them, the guardian of the assembly hall then struck the war-drum that summons men to arms, loud-sounding and adorned with Jāmbūnada gold.
t.1.212.10: Arriving together at Sudharmā, the assembly hall, they told the keeper of the hall all about that bold deed of Pārtha.
t.1.212.12: Then the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, stirred up by that sound, cast aside their food and drink and rushed together into the assembly hall.
t.1.212.14: The tigers among men, the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, took their places by the hundreds upon lion-thrones, like fires upon their altars.
t.1.212.15: When they had sat down together, like the gods in an assembly, the keeper of the hall, along with his attendants, related the deeds of Jiṣṇu.
t.1.212.16: Hearing that, those Vṛṣṇi heroes, the corners of their eyes red with intoxication, sprang up in their pride, unable to endure the deed of Pārtha.
t.1.212.13: Then they took their seats, which had frames of gold and costly coverings, were adorned with gems and coral, and shone with the radiance of blazing fire.
t.1.212.17: "Yoke the chariots quickly, and bring the lances," they cried, "and the costly bows and the massive coats of armor!"
t.1.212.18: Some shouted to the charioteers, "Yoke the chariots!", and some themselves led out the horses adorned with gold.
t.1.212.20: Then the garlanded one, drunk, resembling a peak of Kailāsa, clad in dark-blue garments and swollen with intoxication, spoke these words.
t.1.212.21: What is this you are doing, you fools, while Janārdana remains silent? Without knowing his mind, you are enraged and roar in vain.
t.1.212.19: As chariots, coats of mail and banners were being brought forth, and amid the battle cries of the heroic men, there arose then a great tumult.
t.1.212.22: Let this great-minded one first declare his own intention; whatever is pleasing to him to do, that you should do, unwearied.
t.1.212.23: Then, having heard that speech of acceptable form from Halāyudha, they all fell silent, and then they said, "Well said, well said!"
t.1.212.24: Having heard these fair words of the wise Baladeva, they all sat down once again in the midst of the assembly hall.
t.1.212.25: Then Kāmapāla said to Vāsudeva, the scorcher of foes: “Why do you sit silent, merely looking on, Janārdana?”
t.1.212.26: For your sake, Acyuta, Pārtha was honored by all of us, yet that evil-minded disgrace to his family does not deserve such honor.
t.1.212.27: For what man who considers himself born of a noble family would ever, having eaten food in that very place, break the vessel?
t.1.212.29: Having indeed despised us and having disregarded Keśava, he has today carried off Subhadrā by force, his own death.
t.1.212.28: For who indeed, seeking an alliance and honoring a bond already formed, would, being in earnest a suitor, act with rash violence?
t.1.212.31: Today I alone shall make the earth bereft of the Kauravas, for this transgression of Arjuna is not to be endured by me.
t.1.212.30: How indeed, Govinda, shall I endure this foot planted by him upon the middle of my head, any more than a serpent endures the touch of a foot?
t.1.212.32: As he roared thus, his voice like the thunder of clouds and kettledrums, all the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas then rallied behind him.
